_: BATTLE BOTS: THE MOUTH TABLE. Read by scripts/bots-import-parts.py.
WHY A TABLE AND NOT A PROMPT. Wave one asked the renderer for five mouths on
sixteen head looks. Only the O came back different: smile, grille and zigzag
all came back as the same slatted mouth, because the model has one idea of a
robot mouth and a thin line on a ruler does not argue with it. So the mouth
stops being something we ask for and becomes something we draw, the way the
eye catch light, the wind up key and the coral sole are already drawn.
WHAT THE IMPORTER DOES WITH AN ENTRY. It heals the mouth the render drew back
to clay, cuts this shape into the clay as a recess with the shading named
here, and then hands it to the SAME find_grille and light_grille the file
already ships. Nothing about the lighting is new: the mouth still lands on
GRILLE_LIT, still rides its own value ramp, still sits under the 0.80 ceiling
that keeps it out of find_eyes' sweep, and is still an accent no paint can
reach. Only the shape under the light is ours.
THE DEFAULT IS NO ENTRY. With no mouth named, the importer does exactly what
it did before: it lights the mouth the render drew. Proved by re-deriving the
live catalogue from its raws in a shadow tree, all 80 files, byte identical.
EVERY OUTLINE HERE IS CONVEX ON EVERY ROW, and that is a law rather than a
taste. light_grille recovers a rendered mouth by closing it and then filling
every row from its own leftmost pixel to its own rightmost one, because a
rendered mouth is a letterbox with body coloured prongs standing in it. Hand
that a thin arc and it fills the arc solid; hand it a bare zigzag and it fills
the zigzag into a bar. So a mouth that wants a line in it carries the line as
SHADING INSIDE A ROW CONVEX PLATE, exactly the way the shipped grille carries
its slats. The reward is that the span fill is a no op on every mouth here,
so scripts/sd/rank-part.py, which runs the importer's own find_grille and
light_grille on a candidate, sees exactly the mouth that ships. The importer
refuses any entry whose drawn outline breaks on any row.
GEOMETRY IS MEASURED, NEVER A PIXEL. Every number below is a fraction of the
head's own face: `sep` is the distance between the two eye centres draw_face
found, and `span` is the drop from the eye row to the head's own seat. The
same entry lands correctly on a bear, a cat, a bucket and a TV.
WHAT THE SHEET MEASURED, .bots-preview/sd-shapes2/MOUTHS.png, five mouths on
the eight wave one head shapes, forty heads, no GPU: MOUTH MISPLACED fired
zero times; not one mouth pixel landed in an eye keep out; every mouth landed
wholly on its own head; and find_grille lit exactly the mask the table drew on
all forty, which is the row convexity law holding in practice and not only on
paper. Six of the forty were re-judged DOWN ON THEIR EYES, never their mouth:
judging a file makes the judge measure the exposure again, and the bear and the
bell pair their eyes at exactly one threshold in find_eyes' sweep. The shipped
order finds the eyes once, inside an exposure it fixed first, and does not have
that.
MEASURED ON THE EIGHT WAVE ONE HEADS, which is where drop and the size bands
come from. The mouth the renderer drew sat with its centre 0.520 to 0.652 of
the way from the eye row to the seat (six of the eight between 0.52 and 0.58),
ran 0.30 to 1.16 of the eye separation wide and 0.19 to 0.33 of it tall. Every
width and height here is inside those bands.

law.dropNote: the mouth centre, as a fraction of the drop from the eye row to the head's seat
law.centre: the midpoint of the two eye centres, so the mouth is on the face's own centre and not the canvas'
law.keepOutNote: no mouth pixel may fall within this many eye radii of either eye centre. The eye's own bezel reaches 1.136 radii, so this is the bezel plus a fifth of a radius of clear clay, and the importer refuses the family if one pixel breaks it
law.insideHeadNote: this share of the drawn mouth must land on the head. A mouth that runs off the chin is a refusal, never a trim
law.recessValueNote: the brightest pixel of the authored recess, in value, after the importer's own exposure levelling. find_grille takes the darkest blob at 0.32 or under, so this clears it by 0.06 and the mouth the importer lights is the mouth the table drew. It is a threshold only: light_grille's ramp divides by a percentile of the mouth's own values, so this number cannot change how the mouth looks
law.supersampleNote: the outline is drawn at this multiple and thresholded at half coverage, so the mask is boolean at source resolution exactly as the found mouth's mask is

mouths.name: Grille
mouths.reads: the mouth the game ships today: a wide brass speaker plate with nine slats
notes: THE ONE THAT CHANGES NOTHING. The shipped mouth measures 118 to 131 px wide
with 9 or 10 slats in it, and the eight wave one heads put it at 0.63 to 1.16
of the eye separation. 0.70 by 0.20 with nine slats is that mouth, authored,
so a head can be given the look it already has on any shape.

mouths.name: Smile
mouths.reads: an open, happy mouth: flat along the top, round underneath
notes: NOT A CRESCENT, AND THAT IS THE POINT. A thin smiling arc is two horns on its
top rows, so the span fill would close it into a solid blob and the judge and
the importer would disagree about what shipped. A flat top with a round bottom
is one span on every row, is what an open smiling mouth actually looks like,
and survives the fill untouched. The throat ramp is what stops it reading as a
flat gold sticker: bright at the rim, soft and deep at the middle.

mouths.name: Open O
notes: THE ONE MOUTH THE RENDERER COULD ALREADY DO, and the reason it could is that a
hole is a shape and not a texture. Authored, every head can have it. The bell
head that shipped one measured 0.295 of the eye separation wide; this is a
shade wider and a shade taller than that, because at 0.26 the first sheet
showed it fading into the cheek on the round head.

mouths.name: Zigzag
mouths.reads: a wide plate with one jagged line cut across it
notes: THE LINE IS SHADING IN A PLATE, for the row convexity law above. Taller and
narrower than the grille so the two are told apart by silhouette and not only
by the marks inside them, because at card size the marks are two pixels.

mouths.name: Grin
mouths.reads: a wide open grin, most of the face across, with the top lip shadowed
notes: THE FIFTH, AND IT IS THE SECOND ONE TRIED. The first was a tooth, which the
ramp cannot draw: a bright feature clips at 1.02 of the mouth's own reference
while a dark one has the whole way down to 0.72, so the tooth came back two
percent brighter than the plate and nobody could see it. The second was a
beak, a small wedge narrowing to the chin. It drew perfectly and it failed
for a different reason: at card size a small centred wedge under two big lamp
eyes reads as a NOSE, and the bot then reads as having no mouth at all. That
is the lesson the sheet paid for: a mouth is WIDE. Width is what tells a
mouth from a nose at twenty pixels.
So the fifth is the widest mouth in the table, and the happiest. It is the
smile's shape at nearly half again the width and two thirds the height, which
at card size is a different expression and not a different size of the same
one, and the lip shadow across its top is what keeps a wide shallow bowl from
reading as a gold shield.
